purpose: Valproate is used to help control seizures in people with epilepsy. It is also used to treat bipolar disorder to help stabilize mood swings, and to prevent migraine headaches. Your doctor may prescribe it for one or more of these reasons.
how_it_works: Your brain uses chemical signals to communicate, and sometimes those signals can become overactive, leading to seizures or mood episodes. Valproate works by calming down those overactive signals in the brain. It helps increase a natural calming chemical in the brain called GABA, which helps keep things balanced and under control.
common_side_effects: You may notice nausea, upset stomach, or vomiting, especially when you first start taking it. Some people experience drowsiness, dizziness, or blurry vision. You might also notice hair thinning, weight gain, or mild hand tremors. These often improve over time, but let your doctor know if they bother you.
warnings: This medication can rarely cause serious liver damage or problems with your pancreas, especially in young children or during the first few months of treatment. It must NOT be taken during pregnancy because it can cause serious birth defects and affect the baby's development. Tell your doctor right away if you notice yellowing of your skin or eyes, severe stomach pain, unusual bleeding, or unusual tiredness. Regular blood tests are needed to monitor your liver and blood cell counts while you take this medicine.
typical_dosing: Dosing is very individual and depends on your condition, weight, and how your body responds. For seizures, adults typically start at around 10 to 15 mg per kilogram of body weight per day, split into smaller doses. For bipolar disorder, a common starting dose is 250 mg taken two to three times a day. Your doctor will slowly adjust your dose and use blood tests to make sure the levels are just right for you. Always take it exactly as your doctor instructs.
